key_insight: Disordered metal-oxide photonic glasses can produce the target building-integrated PV colors without strong iridescence, but the achievable color and its stability depend critically on oxide choice, encapsulant, and facade geometry.
engineering_relevance: This work provides a design map for tuning PV module appearance while preserving transparency constraints, helping engineers co-design color with energy generation in building-integrated photovoltaics.
method: Coupled Mie scattering, Percus–Yevick structure factor, and exact phase-function calculations for disordered nanosphere packings.
Included front-glass refraction and absorption using a two-flux transfer model on realistic laminated module stacks.
Swept oxide type, particle size, packing fraction, layer number, encapsulant, and cell technology to match target colors.
evidence_signal: The authors matched four named target colors (blue, green, gold, terracotta) in a three-layer coating with DeltaE00 roughly 0.8–2.5, and quantified viewing-angle/daylight drift of about DeltaE00 5–18.
watch_item: Angle independence is limited in real use: color can shift substantially over the day and with facade viewing geometry, so optical design must be co-optimized for installation conditions.
paper_title: Engineering Color and Angular Stability in Building-Integrated Photovoltaics Using Metal-Oxide Photonic Glasses
